messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Police Officer
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 65

# Vignette: Haunted by What She Couldn't Prevent

Mere has spent forty-one years in uniform. She is the kind of officer other officers call when things go wrong — steady, methodical, unshakeable. Her colleagues in the Pacific Island community policing unit have always known her as the woman who walks toward trouble while everyone else steps back. At seventy-one, she still reports for duty three days a week in a reduced capacity, reviewing case files and mentoring younger constables. She has never once asked for help.

Fourteen months ago, Mere's youngest son, Tama, was struck by a drunk driver while crossing the road outside his home. He survived, but only just. He spent six weeks in intensive care with a traumatic brain injury, two fractured vertebrae, and a shattered pelvis. Mere was the one who received the call. She was the one who identified him on the hospital trolley — his face so swollen she had to look for the small scar on his chin from a childhood fall to be certain it was him. She stood in that corridor in full uniform and did not cry. She told herself she was holding it together for the family. She has not stopped holding it together since, and it is destroying her.

The nights are the worst. Mere lies beside her husband, Rangi, and stares at the ceiling while the image of Tama on that trolley replays itself without her permission. She has tried turning on the television, making tea, reading scripture. Nothing interrupts it. She falls asleep eventually, sometimes past three in the morning, and when she does, she dreams of arriving at accident scenes — scenes she has attended throughout her career — but now it is always Tama's face on the ground, always Tama's body beneath the sheet. She wakes drenched in sweat and lies very still so as not to disturb Rangi, who she has told almost nothing.

At work, she finds herself unable to review any road traffic incident files. She has quietly rerouted them to a junior colleague without explanation. Last month, she was driving to the station when she passed the intersection where Tama was hit. She had driven through it dozens of times since the accident, but that morning something shifted. Her hands locked on the wheel, her vision narrowed, and she pulled to the side of the road and sat there for twenty minutes, unable to move, certain — in a way that felt completely real — that she was about to receive the same phone call all over again. She told no one about this.

Rangi has noticed she is different. He tells her she has become distant, that she flinches when her phone rings, that she no longer wants to visit Tama on Sundays the way she used to. What he does not fully understand is that visiting Tama — watching him relearn words, watching him grip a fork with a hand that once caught a rugby ball — fills Mere with a guilt so profound she can barely breathe in his presence. She was a police officer for four decades. She spent her life protecting people. She was not there to protect her own son.

She carries a particular kind of shame that is common in people who have built their identity around competence and vigilance. She reviews the evening of the accident the way she would review a case file — looking for the moment she could have intervened, the variable she failed to account for. She knows rationally that she could not have known. The rational knowledge changes nothing.

Mere presents now as a woman who is exhausted in a way that sleep does not touch. She is hypervigilant at work — checking and rechecking things she has never needed to check before — and emotionally absent at home. She agreed to attend these sessions only because her GP told her, plainly, that she had no choice. She sat down in the first session, folded her hands in her lap, and said, *"I don't really know why I'm here. I'm fine."*

She is not fine.
